title: OpenAI shuts down the Sora API, ending a $1B Disney video deal and the consumer video experiment
subtitle: The API discontinuation on September 24 closes the last developer entry point to Sora, after the consumer app was sunset in April.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI discontinued the Sora API on September 24, closing the last developer entry point to its text-to-video model. The consumer-facing Sora web app was already sunset in April 2026; the API was the residual surface. According to reporting on the shutdown, the API discontinuation also ends the $1 billion licensing deal that would have brought Marvel and Pixar characters into AI-generated clips through Sora. Existing users were told to export files from sora.chatgpt.com/sunset before the cutoff.

Sora launched in early 2024 as one of the most striking demos in AI: a text-to-video model that could produce a minute of coherent footage from a prompt. The intervening two years have been less kind. Better open-source and closed-source video models (Runway, Google's Veo, Kuaishou's Kling, Meta's Muse Spark) have taken most of the professional workflow share, while consumer video generation has largely migrated to short-form tools inside TikTok, Instagram and CapCut. Sora ended up in an awkward middle: too limited for professional editors, too heavyweight for consumer sharing, and expensive to keep serving.

The Disney partnership is the more interesting casualty. Bringing Marvel and Pixar IP into a general-purpose AI video tool was always going to be a rights minefield — training, safety-filtering, revenue-sharing and character-integrity questions all needed to be answered in ways the underlying tech was not yet stable enough to support. Its unwinding is a signal that the studios and the labs are recalibrating: instead of licensing IP into third-party foundation models, expect more studio-controlled models fine-tuned on their own libraries, with tighter guardrails and clearer distribution paths. Meta's Muse Spark and Alphabet's Veo pipelines are already sketching this direction.

Takeaway for learners: 'flagship demo' and 'durable product' are two very different things, and the graveyard between them is filling up fast. When a lab kills a product this publicly, the useful question is not 'was the underlying model bad?' — Sora's model was good — but 'what did the team learn about distribution, cost, and IP that they now believe?' The next generation of video products from OpenAI will inherit those lessons; the smartest way to read Sora's sunset is as tuition paid.
